extracted.intended_audience: playwrights and literary critics (writers of dramatic poetry / Restoration-era dramatists and educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and judging dramatic poetry/plays: how language, wit, moral tone, and responsiveness to contemporary taste determine a play's merit. The essay contrasts past dramatists with present practice and prescribes refinement and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform your genius to your age
rubrics_metrics.description: They, who have best succeeded on the stage, Have still conformed their genius to their age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful dramatists adapt their work to the manners, wit, and conversation of their own age rather than clinging to outdated modes; examples given: Jonson's mechanical humour suited a duller conversational age. The essay argues that aligning with contemporary tastes is a key factor in theatrical success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withstand meticulous critical scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Think it not envy, that these truths are told; ... when critics weigh Each line, and every word, throughout a play, None of them, no not Jonson in his height, Could pass, without allowing grains for weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern plays must be crafted to survive close inspection by critics who examine each line and word; the author acknowledges critics' thoroughness and treats it as a standard authors must meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement consists of improved wit, language, and conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement of our Wit, Language and Conversation; or, an alteration in them for the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author defines 'refinement' as substantive improvement in wit, language, and everyday conversation; dramatic poetry should reflect and embody this refinement to claim superiority over earlier ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve language by rejecting improper forms and admitting better new words
rubrics_metrics.description: An alteration is made ... either in rejecting such old words, or phrases, which are ill sounding, or improper; or in admitting new, which are more proper, more sounding, and more significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical linguistic standards: remove ill-sounding or improper antiquated words/phrases and accept useful neologisms that are more proper, sonorous, and meaningful. The passage frames this as a central mechanism of linguistic improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must observe and correct linguistic and stylistic errors
rubrics_metrics.description: One testimony of this is undeniable, that we are the first who have observed them; and, certainly, to observe errors is a great step to the correcting of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-awareness of solecisms and flaws is a prerequisite to improvement. The author uses this to justify modern writers' attempts to refine language, claiming earlier writers contained observable errors that moderns can remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiquity alone does not prove excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiquity alone is no plea for the excellency of a poem; but that, one age learning from another, the last ... has the advantage of knowing more and better than the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept a work's quality solely because it is old; evaluate by present standards of skill and refinement. The author invokes Horace and argues that later ages can rightly judge and improve on predecessors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should progress with advances in arts and sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: That poetry may not go backward, when all other arts and sciences are advancing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic poetry ought to share in broader cultural and intellectual progress; stagnation is a vice. The implicit prescription is that playwrights should incorporate contemporary knowledge and sensibilities rather than preserve archaic modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarse comedy; raise themes of love and honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Then comedy was faultless, but 'twas coarse: ... If love and honour now are higher raised, 'Tis not the poet, but the age is praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier comedic successes depended on coarse humor suited to a less refined age; modern drama should eschew such coarseness and emphasize elevated themes (love, honour) in keeping with a more refined audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid solecisms and clear flaws in sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Any man who reads those excellent poets, and compares their language with what is now written, will see it almost in every line; but that this is an improvement ... he will find in every page either some solecism of speech, or some notorious flaw in sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concrete textual standard: minimize grammatical solecisms and lapses in sense. The essay holds that modern writers must reduce such errors relative to predecessors; identifying them is step toward correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to please contemporary (gallant) audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: To please an age more gallant than the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic aim: seek to satisfy the tastes and sensibilities of present audiences (described as 'more gallant'); success is measured in relation to current public conversation and manners rather than past fashions.
